Most of DeWitt's colonial ancestors came over in one great wave.
In 1629 Charles I dissolved Parliament and ruled without it for eleven years, and William Laud,
soon Archbishop of Canterbury, set out to silence the Puritan preachers in the Church of England.
That same year the Massachusetts Bay Company won its royal charter, and in 1630 John Winthrop's fleet of eleven ships
carried about a thousand settlers to Boston, the Reverend John Wilson among them.
Over the next decade some twenty thousand English men, women and children followed,
most of them in family groups from East Anglia, Essex and the West Country: Puritans who meant to worship and govern
themselves as they believed right. Thomas Hooker, silenced at Chelmsford, came in 1633 and three years later led his
congregation west to found Hartford, Thomas Lord and his sons among them.
The Bullards and Uphams, the Parkes, Porters and Hinsdales came in the same years.
Not everyone fitted the Puritan commonwealth: Lawrence and Cassandra Southwick of Salem became Quakers and were driven
out. When the Civil War began in England in 1642, the migration all but stopped.
